chief_complaint: episodic vertigo 3 hours, roaring tinnitus, ear fullness
hpi_details: A 44-year-old female presents to the clinic with episodic vertigo 3 hours, roaring tinnitus, ear fullness. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks extreme work fatigue and poor blood circulation to her head are triggering these dizzy episodes.
concerns: She is worried that she will suffer a sudden violent dizzy spell while driving her kids to school and cause an accident.
expectations: She hopes to get prescription anti-dizziness pills to stop the spinning episodes and a hearing test to check her ear.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Meniere Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Diagnosis requires audiometry documenting sensorineural hearing loss in the appropriate clinical context; management includes dietary/lifestyle counseling and short-term vestibular suppressants only during acute attacks, with diuretics considered selectively.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: A 44-year-old female presents to the clinic with episodic vertigo 3 hours, roaring tinnitus, ear fullness. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Meniere Disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Meniere Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to BPPV without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: focal neurological deficits or asymmetric progressive hearing loss, which suggest stroke or acoustic neuroma rather than typical Meniere disease.
management_principles: Obtain audiometry; provide dietary/lifestyle counseling and short-term vestibular suppressants only during acute attacks, with diuretics considered selectively
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of episodic vertigo 3 hours, roaring tinnitus, ear fullness. HPI: Meniere's disease.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Meniere Disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Presentation consistent with Meniere Disease: episodic vertigo lasting hours accompanied by roaring tinnitus and aural fullness.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain audiometry to assess for sensorineural hearing loss and exclude alternative causes. Counsel on dietary/lifestyle measures; use a vestibular suppressant only briefly during acute attacks. Consider a diuretic with ENT follow-up if attacks persist.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Meniere Disease
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Meniere Disease
Implement evidence-based management plan: audiometry, lifestyle measures, and short-term treatment of acute vertigo attacks

teaching.one_liner: Recurrent vertigo attacks lasting hours with roaring tinnitus and ear fullness.
red_flags: Vertigo accompanied by focal neurological deficits (diplopia, dysarthria, limb weakness/ataxia) — concerning for posterior circulation stroke
Progressive unilateral hearing loss or asymmetric symptoms — raises suspicion for acoustic neuroma

must_ask.say: How long does each episode last?
Any ringing and fullness during attacks?
Has hearing gotten worse over time?
How much salt do you eat?

history.answer: The room has been spinning intensely around me for about three hours now, and my left ear feels clogged up with a loud roaring noise.
The whole world feels like it's spinning around in circles, like I just got off an intense amusement park ride.
This episode started suddenly about three hours ago while I was resting at home, but I've had two similar dizzy spells over the past month.
When these attacks hit me, the severe spinning usually lasts between two and four hours before gradually easing off.
I have had about three of these episodes over the past six weeks, roughly one every couple of weeks.
Moving my head makes the nausea worse, but the spinning didn't start from rolling over in bed or getting up quickly.
Yes, I've had severe nausea since it began and I vomited once about an hour ago.
My left ear feels completely plugged up, and there is a loud roaring sound like rushing water or an ocean wave.
My hearing in my left ear is noticeably muffled right now, especially when people with deep voices speak to me.
I tend to eat salty restaurant meals fairly often, and I drink about three or four cups of strong black coffee every day.
No, I don't have any double vision, trouble speaking, difficulty swallowing, or weakness and numbness in my face, arms, or legs.
No, I haven't had any severe headache or stiffness in my neck.
No, I haven't felt my heart racing, and I have not had any chest tightness or blackouts.
No, I haven't had a cold, fever, sore throat, or runny nose recently.
No dark tarry stools or abnormal bleeding, though I haven't been able to keep much water down today due to the nausea.
I don't have diabetes, and I've never taken insulin or any blood sugar medications.
No, I have never had migraines, and bright lights or normal sounds do not bother me.
No, I have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or irregular heart rhythms.
I haven't started or changed any medications recently; I don't take any prescription drugs at all.
I've been feeling quite fatigued and stressed from long work hours recently, but I wasn't having a panic attack or hyperventilating.
I thought maybe overwork and poor blood circulation to my head were bringing on these terrible dizzy spells.
I'm terrified I'll get one of these violent spinning attacks behind the wheel with my children in the car.
I'm hoping for some reliable anti-dizziness medicine to stop these attacks and a test to see what is going on with my hearing.
I have always been healthy and don't have any chronic medical illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I don't take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or nutritional supplements.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
No, I have never smoked in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of wine when dining with friends, perhaps once or twice a month.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband and son.
There is no family history of ear problems, hearing loss, stroke, or heart disease.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago on my regular monthly cycle, and there is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Supine blood pressure 120/78 mmHg with pulse 74 bpm, and standing blood pressure 118/76 mmHg with pulse 78 bpm, showing no orthostatic drop.
Both external auditory canals are clear and both tympanic membranes are pearly gray, translucent, and normal without perforation or middle ear effusion.
Weber test lateralizes to the right ear and Rinne test is positive bilaterally, consistent with sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear.
Cranial nerves II through XII are intact without facial palsy, ptosis, or dysarthria, aside from diminished hearing acuity in the left ear.

Horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating toward the right ear is present, head impulse test shows subtle corrective saccade on the left, and Dix-Hallpike testing does not elicit paroxysmal positional nystagmus.
Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal bilaterally, but Romberg test shows swaying toward the left with eyes closed.
Heart sounds reveal regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2 and no audible murmurs or gallops.
